label: Divrei HaYamim Bet (2 Chronicles) — Part 1 — Chapters 1–18
summary_plain: Divrei HaYamim Bet opens with Shelomoh asking YHWH for wisdom, not riches or power. YHWH grants him wisdom and adds riches and honor. Shelomoh builds the temple — cedar from Levanon, gold overlays, the great basin called the Sea — and dedicates it with prayer and sacrifice. The glory of YHWH fills the house as a cloud. The Queen of Sheva comes to test Shelomoh with hard questions and is overwhelmed by his wisdom. She says: Happy are your servants who stand before you and hear your wisdom. After Shelomoh's death, the kingdom divides. Rechav'am rules Yehudah. The Chronicler traces the southern kingdom's rulers through reforms and failures.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from DSS fragments and the Orit Ge'ez. The Queen of Sheva narrative (chapter 9) is critical. Sheva (Saba) was an ancient kingdom spanning the southern Arabian Peninsula and the Horn of Africa — modern Yemen, Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Djibouti. The Ethiopian tradition (Kebra Nagast) identifies the Queen of Sheva as Makeda and records that she bore Shelomoh a son, Menelik I, founder of the Solomonic dynasty of Ethiopia. This is not folklore — the Solomonic dynasty ruled Ethiopia from approximately 1270 to 1974 CE. The Aksumite Empire (c. 100-940 CE) controlled both sides of the Red Sea, including Saba. The trade corridor between Yisra'EL and Sheva was the African-Arabian spice and incense route — a continuous commercial and cultural connection. The Orit Ge'ez preserves the Sheva connection as living tradition. The Great Eraser separates Ethiopia from Yisra'EL by treating the Red Sea as a continental boundary when it is actually a narrow waterway that connected, not divided, the African and Arabian shores.

key_terms.definition: The construction and dedication of the Temple in Yerushalayim — the central event of Divrei HaYamim Bet, narrated at length across six chapters
Shlomo's extended prayer at the Temple dedication, calling on YHWH to hear prayers made toward this place, especially in times of defeat, drought, famine, plague, or exile

key_terms.term: 'If My People Called by My Name'
key_terms.definition: YHWH's answer to Shlomo's prayer — unique to Divrei HaYamim, not in Melakhim: 'if my people who are called by my name humble themselves and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven'
When Shlomo finished praying, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices — YHWH's acceptance of the Temple dedication
Rekhav'am's refusal to lighten the people's burden leads the northern tribes to reject his rule — 'What portion have we in David? Every man to your tents, O Yisra'el!'
Shlomo's son who becomes king; ignores the elders' counsel and follows the young men's advice to increase the people's yoke — the direct cause of the kingdom's split
The northern leader who leads the ten tribes away from Rekhav'am's rule, establishing the northern kingdom with golden calves at Beit-El and Dan
Asa removes the foreign altars, smashes sacred pillars, cuts down the Asherim, commands Yehudah to seek YHWH — a covenant reform king in the Davidic line
Yehoshafat sends priests and Levites throughout Yehudah to teach Torah; builds fortified cities; defeats a great coalition through prayer and prophetic word — YHWH fights for them
Yehoshafat's son who married Akhav's daughter; killed his brothers; built high places; Yisra'el went astray under him — received a letter of condemnation from Eliyahu the prophet

faq.question: What is the significance of YHWH's fire descending on the Temple sacrifice?
faq.answer: It is YHWH's direct acceptance of the Temple — the same pattern as YHWH's fire at Mosheh's first sacrifice (Vayikra 9:24) and Eliyahu's sacrifice on Mount Karmel. Fire from heaven is the covenant sign of YHWH's presence and approval.

faq.question: Why is 2 Divrei HaYamim 7:14 significant as a unique text?
faq.answer: The verse 'If my people who are called by my name...' appears only in Divrei HaYamim, not in the parallel account in Melakhim. It is YHWH's direct conditional promise of restoration — heard and preserved only in this text.

faq.question: What caused the kingdom to split?
faq.answer: Rekhav'am rejected the counsel of the experienced elders who told him to lighten the people's burden. Following younger advisors, he threatened to increase it. The northern tribes declared 'What portion have we in David?' and withdrew under Yarov'am.

faq.question: What is the theological significance of Yehoshafat's battle strategy?
faq.answer: Yehoshafat sends singers praising YHWH ahead of the army — when they begin to sing, YHWH sets an ambush against the enemy coalition and they destroy each other. YHWH fights; Yehudah collects the spoil for three days.

faq.question: What makes Zerakh's army notable in ch.14?
faq.answer: Zerakh the Kushite (Ethiopian) comes against Asa with a million men and 300 chariots — an enormous force. Asa's prayer of dependence on YHWH alone results in YHWH defeating the entire army.

faq.question: How does Divrei HaYamim Bet evaluate the kings of Yehudah?
faq.answer: Each king is evaluated by whether he sought YHWH and kept the covenant. Reform kings (Asa, Yehoshafat, Khizkiyahu, Yoshiyahu) are praised at length; apostate kings are condemned and their reigns summarized briefly.

faq.question: Why does Divrei HaYamim Bet omit the story of David and Bat-Sheva?
faq.answer: Divrei HaYamim's concern is the Temple cult and covenant worship, not the full political history. It presents an idealized David as the Temple's founder. David's moral failures are outside the book's theological focus.

faq.question: What is the importance of the Torah-teaching mission in Yehoshafat's reign?
faq.answer: Yehoshafat sends priests and Levites with the Book of Torah to teach throughout all of Yehudah — the first explicit national Torah-education program. This reflects Divrei HaYamim's concern that all of Yehudah knows and follows YHWH's covenant.

faq.question: What letter does Yehoram receive from Eliyahu?
faq.answer: A written letter condemning Yehoram for walking in the way of the kings of Yisra'el, for killing his brothers who were better than he was, and predicting that YHWH would strike him and his people with a great plague — and that Yehoram would die of a severe bowel disease.

faq.question: How does the golden calf worship of Yarov'am affect the northern kingdom in Divrei HaYamim's view?
faq.answer: By placing golden calves at Beit-El and Dan and driving out the Levitical priests, Yarov'am cut the northern kingdom off from legitimate covenant worship. Levites and those who sought YHWH from all the tribes migrated to Yehudah — concentrating covenant faithfulness in the south.
